expectedText:
APPORTIONMENT OF A SEPARATE-PROPERTY RESIDENCE PAID DOWN WITH COMMUNITY FUNDS (MOORE/MARSDEN) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

PURPOSE AND IDENTIFICATION OF THE RESIDENCE
This document concerns the real property located at 1234 Elm Street, Sacramento, CA 95814 (the "residence"), which Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee owned before their marriage, or otherwise holds or claims to hold as separate property, and on which payments were made during the marriage, in connection with the dissolution of their marriage. The parties married on June 14, 2015 and separated on March 2, 2026. It states legal background on how California courts have apportioned, between the community and the owning spouse's separate estate, the equity and appreciation in a separate-property residence whose purchase-money loan was paid down with community funds -- the approach commonly called the Moore/Marsden rule -- together with the general community and separate property statutes from which that case law proceeds and the later published decisions applying it to post-separation payments and to property purchased during marriage with mixed funds. This document is not a court order, is not an appraisal or valuation of the residence, and does not state whether any part of the residence's equity or appreciation is community property, separate property, or a combination of both.

GENERAL RULE: PROPERTY OWNED BEFORE MARRIAGE IS SEPARATE PROPERTY
By statute, the separate property of a married person includes all property owned by the person before marriage, all property acquired after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent, and the rents, issues, and profits of that property. A residence one spouse bought before the marriage therefore starts as that spouse's separate property. That starting point, rather than the form of title, is what makes the Moore/Marsden apportionment question arise when community funds are later used to pay the loan on the residence.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "(a) Separate property of a married person includes all of the following: (1) All property owned by the person before marriage. (2) All property acquired by the person after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent. (3) The rents, issues, and profits of the property described in this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 770 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (a), the definition of a married person's separate property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=770.)
  Known gap: This is a single, general statutory definition (Cal. Fam. Code § 770(a)) and is subject to other statutes and to the case law on tracing, commingling, and transmutation that are outside the scope of this clause. The separate character of the residence at acquisition does not by itself determine how appreciation during the marriage, or equity built with community loan payments, is characterized; that is the subject of the case-law clauses in this document.

GENERAL RULE: PROPERTY ACQUIRED DURING MARRIAGE IS COMMUNITY PROPERTY
As a general rule, all property acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in California is community property, except as otherwise provided by statute. Earnings from a spouse's labor during the marriage fall within this rule, which is why loan payments made from those earnings are community contributions to whatever they are used to buy or pay down.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Except as otherwise provided by statute, all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in this state is community property."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 760 (California Legislative Information text), the general definition of community property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=760.)
  Known gap: This is a single, general statutory rule (Cal. Fam. Code § 760) subject to numerous statutory exceptions that are outside the scope of this clause. It does not itself resolve how a separate-property residence paid down with community earnings is apportioned; the case-law clauses in this document address that question.

GENERAL RULE: THE COMMUNITY ESTATE IS DIVIDED EQUALLY AT DISSOLUTION
In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation, the court divides the community estate of the parties equally, except upon the parties' written agreement or oral stipulation in open court, or as otherwise provided in the Family Code division governing property division. A community interest in an otherwise separate residence, once determined under the Moore/Marsden rule, is part of the community estate that this equal-division rule governs; the separate share is confirmed to the owning spouse.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Except upon the written agreement of the parties, or on oral stipulation of the parties in open court, or as otherwise provided in this division, in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, the court shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2550 (California Legislative Information text), the equal-division rule for the community estate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2550.)
  Known gap: This states only the general equal-division mandate of Cal. Fam. Code § 2550. The statute's own exceptions (written agreement, oral stipulation in open court, and other provisions of Division 7 of the Family Code) and the separate rules on valuation date and reimbursement are not described here. Mohler (2020), described in later clauses, cites sections 770 and 2550 together for the proposition that community property is divided equally while separate property is awarded to its owner.

CASE LAW: MOORE -- COMMUNITY LOAN PAYMENTS ON A PRE-MARRIAGE RESIDENCE CREATE A PRO TANTO COMMUNITY PROPERTY INTEREST
In In re Marriage of Moore (1980), the California Supreme Court addressed a house one spouse purchased before marriage, taking title in her own name, on which loan payments were later made with community funds during the marriage. The court applied the rule, developed through earlier California decisions, that where community funds are used to make payments on property purchased by one spouse before marriage, the community acquires a pro tanto community property interest in the property in the ratio that the payments on the purchase price made with community funds bear to the payments made with separate funds. In a footnote, the court added that although the trial court had labeled the community's interest an equitable charge, under California law the interest is properly characterized as a community property interest in the house. Later decisions treat this as the first half of what is now called the Moore/Marsden rule: the community's interest grows as community funds reduce the loan principal, even though title remains in the owning spouse's name.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "a pro tanto community property interest in such property in the ratio that the payments on the purchase price with community funds bear to the payments made with separate funds"
  — In re Marriage of Moore (1980) 28 Cal.3d 366, 28 Cal.3d 366, 371-372 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1391694/in-re-marriage-of-moore/)
  "it is clear under California law that the interest is properly characterized as a community property interest in the house"
  — In re Marriage of Moore (1980) 28 Cal.3d 366, 28 Cal.3d 366, 371, fn. 1 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1391694/in-re-marriage-of-moore/)
  "In In re Marriage of Moore (1980) 28 Cal.3d 366, 371-372 (Moore), our Supreme Court held that where community funds are used to pay down the principal owed on a loan on property purchased by one spouse before marriage, the community obtains "'a pro tanto community property interest in such property in the ratio that the payments on the purchase price with community funds bear to the payments made with separate funds.' [Citations.]""
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  Known gap: This describes the California Supreme Court's decision as characterized in In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788 and In re Marriage of Bonvino (2015) 241 Cal.App.4th 1411, which quote the passages set out here; the pro tanto formulation is itself Moore's quotation of earlier decisions. Pin cites (pp. 371-372 and p. 371, fn. 1) are taken from Mohler's citations. Moore also addressed other issues (including the treatment of the parties' equity and the fair market value of the house before and after marriage) that are not described here. CASE LAW: MOORE -- THE COMMUNITY'S PERCENTAGE IS COMMUNITY PRINCIPAL REDUCTION DIVIDED BY THE PURCHASE PRICE; INTEREST, TAXES, AND INSURANCE DO NOT COUNT
Moore approved a specific method for measuring the respective interests. The community's percentage interest is found by dividing the amount by which community property payments reduced the loan principal by the purchase price of the property; the separate estate's percentage is the balance, reflecting the down payment, the loan proceeds, and any separate principal payments. Each estate's share of the appreciation during the marriage is that percentage multiplied by the appreciation, and each estate's total share is its capital contribution plus its share of appreciation. The court held that amounts paid for interest, taxes, and insurance do not contribute to the capital investment and are not considered part of it, so those payments -- often the bulk of a monthly mortgage payment -- do not increase the community's percentage. In Moore's own figures, $5,986.20 of community principal reduction was divided by the $56,640 purchase price. Bonvino (2015) restated the same steps: divide the community's principal reduction by the purchase price, multiply by the total appreciation during marriage, and add back the community's equity payments; amounts that do not increase equity, including interest, taxes, and insurance, are excluded.

  — In re Marriage of Moore (1980) 28 Cal.3d 366, 28 Cal.3d 366, 372 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1391694/in-re-marriage-of-moore/)

CASE LAW: MARSDEN -- APPRECIATION BEFORE THE MARRIAGE IS CREDITED TO THE SEPARATE ESTATE, AND THE FORMULA RUNS FROM THE PURCHASE PRICE
In In re Marriage of Marsden (1982), the Court of Appeal applied Moore to a residence the husband had acquired in 1962, years before the marriage, that had already appreciated substantially by the wedding date. The husband argued that the separate estate's percentage should be based on the property's fair market value at the time of marriage ($65,000) rather than the 1962 purchase price ($38,300). The court observed that the Moore/Lucas/Aufmuth formula makes no provision for prenuptial appreciation and therefore offers no guidance on the point, but concluded that it is equitable to credit the separate property interest with the prenuptial appreciation, while noting that it was bound by the Moore/Lucas/Aufmuth formula and that any adjustments must fit within that formula. As Mohler (2020) later summarized, Marsden supplemented Moore by establishing that the separate owner is awarded the pre-marriage appreciation, but did not fold that appreciation into the percentage calculation, which remains tied to the original purchase price: the community's percentage is applied only to the appreciation occurring during the marriage, and the appreciation before the marriage stays with the separate owner.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "The Moore/Lucas/Aufmuth formula makes no provision for prenuptial appreciation on property and therefore offers no guidance."
  — In re Marriage of Marsden (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 426, 130 Cal.App.3d 426, 438-439 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2108735/in-re-marriage-of-marsden/)

  — In re Marriage of Marsden (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 426, 130 Cal.App.3d 426, 438-439 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2108735/in-re-marriage-of-marsden/)
  "In re Marriage of Marsden (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 426, 437 (Marsden) supplemented Moore's calculation by establishing that the owner of the separate property should be awarded the pre-marriage appreciation in the property's value."

  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)

CASE LAW: MOHLER -- HOW THE MOORE/MARSDEN RULE MEASURES THE COMMUNITY'S SHARE
In In re Marriage of Mohler (2020), the Court of Appeal restated the Moore/Marsden rule as applied to a home one spouse owned before marriage whose mortgage the community paid during the marriage. As the court described it, Moore uses the original purchase price as the reference point for a 100 percent interest in the property, attributes the entire purchase-price value to the separate owner as the marriage begins, and thereafter measures the community's growing interest by dividing the amount by which community payments reduced the loan principal by the purchase price. The court explained that the denominator is the purchase price -- not the owner's out-of-pocket funds and not the fair market value at the date of marriage -- and that the numerator is the amount by which community funds reduced the principal; funds used for interest, taxes, or maintenance do not enter the calculation. Following Marsden and In re Marriage of Frick (1986), the court summarized the community's share in the property's value at the end of the marriage as the sum of (a) the share of appreciation during the marriage attributable to community funds under the Moore formula and (b) the principal payments the community made, which are returned to the community. In Mohler's own figures, $56,557 of community principal payments on a home purchased for $168,000 gave the community a 33.66 percent interest as of separation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Thus, as the community makes payments during the marriage that reduce the principal owed on the separate property, the community acquires a beneficial interest in that property, even if title remains in the name of the original owner."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  "Funds used for interest, taxes, or maintenance are inapposite to the calculation."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  "This ultimately means that the community's share in the value of the property at the end of a marriage can be determined by adding together (a) the amount of capital appreciation during the marriage that is attributable to community funds under the Moore formula and (b) the principal payments made by the community funds, which are returned to the community."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Mohler's description of the rule rather than the underlying Moore and Marsden opinions, which are described separately in this document. Mohler's summary of the calculation cites In re Marriage of Frick (1986) 181 Cal.App.3d 997, which this project has not independently verified. The CourtListener text used for verification is the certified-for-publication slip opinion (filed April 13, 2020), which lacks Official Reports pagination; pin cites to 47 Cal.App.5th are therefore omitted for Mohler throughout this document. Mohler also notes, citing In re Marriage of Nelson (2006) 139 Cal.App.4th 1546, that a separate-property owner is not credited under Moore/Marsden for the community's benefit in living in the home; Nelson is not independently verified here.

CASE LAW: MOHLER -- THE COMMUNITY'S PERCENTAGE STOPS GROWING AT SEPARATION, BUT IT SHARES IN APPRECIATION THROUGH TRIAL
Mohler held that it was error to continue increasing the community's Moore/Marsden percentage on account of mortgage principal the owning spouse paid after the date of separation from separate earnings. The court reasoned that Moore/Marsden rests on the idea that community property is being invested in the separate asset by creating equity in it, so only community funds that reduce loan principal count; after separation, a spouse's earnings and accumulations are separate property under Family Code section 771(a), and post-separation principal payments from separate property no more enlarge the community's interest than the owner's pre-marriage principal payments did. The court stated that the rule applies only insofar as community funds are used to build equity, a situation that often ends at separation. At the same time, the court confirmed that the property is valued as of the date of trial under Family Code section 2552(a), and that the community's percentage interest fixed at separation shares proportionally in the property's increase in equity through the time of trial -- in Mohler's example, 33.66 percent of a $345,000 increase measured from the marriage date to trial, plus return of the $56,557 in community principal payments.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "We hold that this was error. The Moore/Marsden rule applies only insofar as community funds are used to build equity in an asset, a situation which often terminates, as it did here, upon separation."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  "Just as Greg's pre-marriage reduction of loan principal did not increase the community's interest under Moore/Marsden, neither do his post-separation payments from his separate property."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  "When the trial court determines the value of the community's property interest in a residence, the property is to be valued as of the date of trial, not as of the date of the parties' separation."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  "The community had a beneficial 33.66 percent interest in the property at the time of separation, and it shares proportionally in the equity increase in the property through the time of trial."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  Known gap: This clause describes a single published Court of Appeal decision (Fourth Appellate District, Division Two) reached on undisputed figures; the parties agreed on the community's percentage as of separation, and the only dispute was whether post-separation payments should enlarge it. Mohler's citation of Family Code section 2552 for the trial-date valuation rule, and its reference to a party's ability to seek an alternate valuation date, are described from the opinion and not independently verified here. The opinion's text at one point cites "Fam. Code § 2252, subd. (b)" for the alternate-valuation-date procedure, which appears to be a typographical reference to section 2552(b); this document does not rely on that passage. CASE LAW: MOHLER -- POST-SEPARATION OCCUPANCY IS ADDRESSED THROUGH WATTS CHARGES DISCOUNTED TO THE COMMUNITY'S PARTIAL INTEREST
Mohler held, as a matter of first impression, that so-called Watts charges -- the equitable charge against a spouse for the reasonable value of exclusive post-separation use of a community asset -- may be applied where the community does not own the residence outright but holds a partial beneficial interest under a Moore/Marsden calculation. The court described the concept as the same as when the community holds title, but with the amount charged discounted to reflect the community's partial interest. It outlined an approach for the trial court on remand: determine the net rental profit the property would have produced during the owning spouse's post-separation occupancy (expected rent less mortgage, taxes, insurance, maintenance, and repair), then charge the occupying spouse the community's percentage (there, 33.66 percent) of that net profit for the period between separation and trial, while leaving the trial court its equitable discretion over whether and how much to charge. The court characterized this as a different legal concept from Moore/Marsden, which it said was the wrong vehicle for compensating the community for post-separation occupancy.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "We conclude that Watts charges may be applied where, as here, the community does not own the property outright but instead maintains a beneficial partial interest in the property due to a Moore/Marsden calculation."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  "The concept is precisely the same as Watts charges when the community maintains title to the home, but with the amount charged discounted for the fact that the community maintains only a partial interest in the property for purposes of dividing the property upon a marital dissolution."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  "If the husband obtained a benefit from the community through living in the house beyond the parties' separation date, the trial court may account for this through so-called Watts charges, a different legal concept than the Moore/Marsden rule."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  Known gap: This is the holding of a single published Court of Appeal decision, and the court expressly left the precise Watts calculation to the trial court on remand and disclaimed any intent to constrain the trial court's equitable discretion. Watts charges and Epstein credits are addressed in more detail in this project's separate Watts/Epstein information sheet; the underlying decisions (In re Marriage of Watts (1985) 171 Cal.App.3d 366; In re Marriage of Epstein (1979) 24 Cal.3d 76) are cited from Mohler and not re-verified here. Pin cites are omitted because the verified text is the slip opinion.

CASE LAW: MOHLER'S SUMMARY OF RELATED SITUATIONS -- REFINANCING AND CAPITAL IMPROVEMENTS
Mohler noted that later decisions have addressed more complicated variations of the Moore/Marsden rule. As summarized by the court, the community is entitled to an interest in the property when the spouses refinance a separate property and pay off the original mortgage with a new loan (citing In re Marriage of Branco (1996)), and the community is entitled to reimbursement when its funds are used for capital improvements to a separate property (citing In re Marriage of Allen (2002)). Mohler itself involved only a straightforward calculation in which the community's interest could be computed by dividing the principal paid during the marriage by the original purchase price.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "For example, the community is entitled to an interest in the property when the spouses refinance a separate property and pay off the original mortgage with a new loan (In re Marriage of Branco (1996) 47 Cal.App.4th 1621, 1629), and the community is entitled to reimbursement when its funds are used for capital improvements to a separate property (In re Marriage of Allen (2002) 96 Cal.App.4th 497, 501)."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  "This case concerns only a straightforward Moore/Marsden calculation, where the community's interest in the Lomello property can be calculated simply by dividing the amount of principal paid during the marriage by the original purchase price."
  — In re Marriage of Mohler (2020) 47 Cal.App.5th 788, 47 Cal.App.5th 788 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4744571/marriage-of-mohler/)
  Known gap: This clause reports Mohler's one-sentence characterization of Branco and Allen; neither of those decisions has been independently fetched or verified by this project, and their holdings are more detailed than Mohler's summary. How a refinance loan is characterized (including the lender-intent rules described in the Bonvino clause) and how an improvement-based claim is measured are outside the verified scope of this document. Pin cites are omitted because the verified text is the slip opinion.

CASE LAW: BONVINO -- PROPERTY BOUGHT DURING MARRIAGE WITH A SEPARATE DOWN PAYMENT AND COMMUNITY LOAN PROCEEDS TAKES PROPORTIONATE INTERESTS ABSENT A WRITTEN TRANSMUTATION
In In re Marriage of Bonvino (2015), a home was purchased during the marriage with a down payment from the husband's separate funds and the proceeds of a loan in his name, with title taken in his name as his sole and separate property; he later paid off the loan with proceeds from selling a home he had owned before marriage. The Court of Appeal held, in the published portion of its opinion, that when property is acquired during marriage with both separate and community funds, the transmutation requirements of Family Code section 852 must be satisfied before the reimbursement provisions of section 2640 apply; because no document contained an express written transmutation, the husband's traceable separate contributions kept their separate character and both separate and community interests were established in the property in proportion to their contributions under the formula of In re Marriage of Aufmuth (1979) and Moore. The court explained that section 2640 by its plain language applies only to separate contributions to the acquisition of community property. Bonvino also applied the lender-intent rule to the purchase loan: loan proceeds acquired during marriage are presumed community property, the presumption may be rebutted by showing the lender intended to rely solely on the borrowing spouse's separate property, and the husband had not carried that burden, so the loan proceeds were community contributions. Bonvino described Moore's method in the same terms as Mohler, including that amounts that do not increase equity -- interest, taxes, and insurance -- are excluded from the calculation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "In the published portion of the opinion, we hold that if property is acquired during marriage with both separate and community funds, the transmutation requirements of section 852 must be satisfied before the reimbursement provisions of section 2640 apply."
  — In re Marriage of Bonvino (2015) 241 Cal.App.4th 1411, 241 Cal.App.4th 1411 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3153709/marriage-of-bonvino/)
  "By the plain language of the statute, section 2640 applies to contributions to the acquisition of community property."
  — In re Marriage of Bonvino (2015) 241 Cal.App.4th 1411, 241 Cal.App.4th 1411 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3153709/marriage-of-bonvino/)
  "Husband's traceable separate property investment retained its separate property character, and both separate and community property interests were established in the property in accordance with the formula established in Aufmuth and Moore."
  — In re Marriage of Bonvino (2015) 241 Cal.App.4th 1411, 241 Cal.App.4th 1411 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3153709/marriage-of-bonvino/)
  "Loan proceeds acquired during marriage are presumed to be community property."
  — In re Marriage of Bonvino (2015) 241 Cal.App.4th 1411, 241 Cal.App.4th 1411 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3153709/marriage-of-bonvino/)
  "Amounts that do not increase the equity value of the property, including interest, taxes and insurance, are not included in the calculation of the parties' interests in the property."
  — In re Marriage of Bonvino (2015) 241 Cal.App.4th 1411, 241 Cal.App.4th 1411 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3153709/marriage-of-bonvino/)
  Known gap: This is a single published decision (Second Appellate District, Division Five), certified for partial publication; the portions addressing the quitclaim deed, rental-value charges, and sanctions are unpublished and not described here. Bonvino's facts differ from the classic Moore/Marsden case in that the property was bought during the marriage, and its holding turns on the interplay of sections 852, 2581, and 2640 -- topics covered in more depth by this project's separate transmutation, joint-title presumption, and section 2640 information sheets. The lender-intent authorities Bonvino relies on (In re Marriage of Grinius (1985) 166 Cal.App.3d 1179; Bank of California v. expectedJSON.body: This document concerns the real property located at 1234 Elm Street, Sacramento, CA 95814 (the "residence"), which Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee owned before their marriage, or otherwise holds or claims to hold as separate property, and on which payments were made during the marriage, in connection with the dissolution of their marriage. The parties married on June 14, 2015 and separated on March 2, 2026. It states legal background on how California courts have apportioned, between the community and the owning spouse's separate estate, the equity and appreciation in a separate-property residence whose purchase-money loan was paid down with community funds -- the approach commonly called the Moore/Marsden rule -- together with the general community and separate property statutes from which that case law proceeds and the later published decisions applying it to post-separation payments and to property purchased during marriage with mixed funds. This document is not a court order, is not an appraisal or valuation of the residence, and does not state whether any part of the residence's equity or appreciation is community property, separate property, or a combination of both.

By statute, the separate property of a married person includes all property owned by the person before marriage, all property acquired after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent, and the rents, issues, and profits of that property. A residence one spouse bought before the marriage therefore starts as that spouse's separate property. That starting point, rather than the form of title, is what makes the Moore/Marsden apportionment question arise when community funds are later used to pay the loan on the residence.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Moore (1980), the California Supreme Court addressed a house one spouse purchased before marriage, taking title in her own name, on which loan payments were later made with community funds during the marriage. The court applied the rule, developed through earlier California decisions, that where community funds are used to make payments on property purchased by one spouse before marriage, the community acquires a pro tanto community property interest in the property in the ratio that the payments on the purchase price made with community funds bear to the payments made with separate funds. In a footnote, the court added that although the trial court had labeled the community's interest an equitable charge, under California law the interest is properly characterized as a community property interest in the house. Later decisions treat this as the first half of what is now called the Moore/Marsden rule: the community's interest grows as community funds reduce the loan principal, even though title remains in the owning spouse's name.

expectedJSON.body: Moore approved a specific method for measuring the respective interests. The community's percentage interest is found by dividing the amount by which community property payments reduced the loan principal by the purchase price of the property; the separate estate's percentage is the balance, reflecting the down payment, the loan proceeds, and any separate principal payments. Each estate's share of the appreciation during the marriage is that percentage multiplied by the appreciation, and each estate's total share is its capital contribution plus its share of appreciation. The court held that amounts paid for interest, taxes, and insurance do not contribute to the capital investment and are not considered part of it, so those payments -- often the bulk of a monthly mortgage payment -- do not increase the community's percentage. In Moore's own figures, $5,986.20 of community principal reduction was divided by the $56,640 purchase price. Bonvino (2015) restated the same steps: divide the community's principal reduction by the purchase price, multiply by the total appreciation during marriage, and add back the community's equity payments; amounts that do not increase equity, including interest, taxes, and insurance, are excluded.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Marsden (1982), the Court of Appeal applied Moore to a residence the husband had acquired in 1962, years before the marriage, that had already appreciated substantially by the wedding date. The husband argued that the separate estate's percentage should be based on the property's fair market value at the time of marriage ($65,000) rather than the 1962 purchase price ($38,300). The court observed that the Moore/Lucas/Aufmuth formula makes no provision for prenuptial appreciation and therefore offers no guidance on the point, but concluded that it is equitable to credit the separate property interest with the prenuptial appreciation, while noting that it was bound by the Moore/Lucas/Aufmuth formula and that any adjustments must fit within that formula. As Mohler (2020) later summarized, Marsden supplemented Moore by establishing that the separate owner is awarded the pre-marriage appreciation, but did not fold that appreciation into the percentage calculation, which remains tied to the original purchase price: the community's percentage is applied only to the appreciation occurring during the marriage, and the appreciation before the marriage stays with the separate owner.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Mohler (2020), the Court of Appeal restated the Moore/Marsden rule as applied to a home one spouse owned before marriage whose mortgage the community paid during the marriage. As the court described it, Moore uses the original purchase price as the reference point for a 100 percent interest in the property, attributes the entire purchase-price value to the separate owner as the marriage begins, and thereafter measures the community's growing interest by dividing the amount by which community payments reduced the loan principal by the purchase price. The court explained that the denominator is the purchase price -- not the owner's out-of-pocket funds and not the fair market value at the date of marriage -- and that the numerator is the amount by which community funds reduced the principal; funds used for interest, taxes, or maintenance do not enter the calculation. Following Marsden and In re Marriage of Frick (1986), the court summarized the community's share in the property's value at the end of the marriage as the sum of (a) the share of appreciation during the marriage attributable to community funds under the Moore formula and (b) the principal payments the community made, which are returned to the community. In Mohler's own figures, $56,557 of community principal payments on a home purchased for $168,000 gave the community a 33.66 percent interest as of separation.

expectedJSON.body: Mohler held that it was error to continue increasing the community's Moore/Marsden percentage on account of mortgage principal the owning spouse paid after the date of separation from separate earnings. The court reasoned that Moore/Marsden rests on the idea that community property is being invested in the separate asset by creating equity in it, so only community funds that reduce loan principal count; after separation, a spouse's earnings and accumulations are separate property under Family Code section 771(a), and post-separation principal payments from separate property no more enlarge the community's interest than the owner's pre-marriage principal payments did. The court stated that the rule applies only insofar as community funds are used to build equity, a situation that often ends at separation. At the same time, the court confirmed that the property is valued as of the date of trial under Family Code section 2552(a), and that the community's percentage interest fixed at separation shares proportionally in the property's increase in equity through the time of trial -- in Mohler's example, 33.66 percent of a $345,000 increase measured from the marriage date to trial, plus return of the $56,557 in community principal payments.

expectedJSON.body: Mohler held, as a matter of first impression, that so-called Watts charges -- the equitable charge against a spouse for the reasonable value of exclusive post-separation use of a community asset -- may be applied where the community does not own the residence outright but holds a partial beneficial interest under a Moore/Marsden calculation. The court described the concept as the same as when the community holds title, but with the amount charged discounted to reflect the community's partial interest. It outlined an approach for the trial court on remand: determine the net rental profit the property would have produced during the owning spouse's post-separation occupancy (expected rent less mortgage, taxes, insurance, maintenance, and repair), then charge the occupying spouse the community's percentage (there, 33.66 percent) of that net profit for the period between separation and trial, while leaving the trial court its equitable discretion over whether and how much to charge. The court characterized this as a different legal concept from Moore/Marsden, which it said was the wrong vehicle for compensating the community for post-separation occupancy.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Bonvino (2015), a home was purchased during the marriage with a down payment from the husband's separate funds and the proceeds of a loan in his name, with title taken in his name as his sole and separate property; he later paid off the loan with proceeds from selling a home he had owned before marriage. The Court of Appeal held, in the published portion of its opinion, that when property is acquired during marriage with both separate and community funds, the transmutation requirements of Family Code section 852 must be satisfied before the reimbursement provisions of section 2640 apply; because no document contained an express written transmutation, the husband's traceable separate contributions kept their separate character and both separate and community interests were established in the property in proportion to their contributions under the formula of In re Marriage of Aufmuth (1979) and Moore. The court explained that section 2640 by its plain language applies only to separate contributions to the acquisition of community property. Bonvino also applied the lender-intent rule to the purchase loan: loan proceeds acquired during marriage are presumed community property, the presumption may be rebutted by showing the lender intended to rely solely on the borrowing spouse's separate property, and the husband had not carried that burden, so the loan proceeds were community contributions. Bonvino described Moore's method in the same terms as Mohler, including that amounts that do not increase equity -- interest, taxes, and insurance -- are excluded from the calculation.
